description:
We are TEAM ASCENT, 

led by Abhishek VK alongside Akbar Ali M, Arjun Krishna K, Adharsh K, Aswin R, and Ranjith PG, six student innovators passionate about aerospace and STEM education. Inspired by the Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer challenge, we collaborated across NASA telemetry integration, Vite front-end engineering, and educational game design to turn complex lunar and Martian survival physics into an intuitive, replayable mission simulator for young explorers.
summary:
Space exploration requires mastering complex engineering trade-offs, but these concepts are often too abstract or complicated for young learners. To bridge this gap, we developed OrbitOps, an interactive web application built with Java that acts as a Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer for children ages 7–12.

Our app addresses the challenge by transforming real-world lunar mission constraints into an engaging, gamified experience. Players step into the shoes of a mission commander managing a lunar outpost, where they must carefully balance vital resources like solar power management during lunar night cycles, life support, and radiation shielding. Every decision carries a direct consequence, teaching players authentic systems-thinking and resource management. This project is important because early exposure to STEM through interactive problem-solving sparks curiosity and builds the next generation of space explorers. 
By leveraging Java for a robust, reliable backend, our web app delivers seamless performance and smooth gameplay straight to the browser making lunar mission training accessible, interactive, and fun for classrooms everywhere.
details:
Project OrbitOps: AstroBase – Junior Flight Director

What It Does & How It Works Project OrbitOps is an interactive, browser-based mission simulation game designed to train young learners (ages 7–12) as Junior Flight Directors managing an Artemis lunar outpost. Across a 5-Sol mission cycle, players balance competing survival systems—Power Reserves, Oxygen Supply, Water Reserves, and Science Progress—while managing a three-person crew (Commander, Flight Engineer, and Life Support Specialist) across specialized habitat modules (Habitat, Greenhouse, Science Lab, Solar Array, and Storm Vault).

The simulation dynamically integrates real-world aerospace data—including live space weather telemetry via the NASA DONKI Space Weather API (tracking Coronal Mass Ejections and solar storm activity), surface cartography from the NASA Planetary Data System (PDS), atmospheric telemetry from NASA Mars Rover Environmental Data, and NASA Artemis Base Camp life-support parameters—to scale mission hazards in real time. During each Sol, players face unscripted emergencies such as Solar Particle Events (SEPs), dust-covered solar arrays, water recycler failures, and module oxygen leaks. Players must choose between competing operational trade-offs—such as sheltering the crew to prevent radiation exposure at the cost of halting scientific research, or sealing off a leaking habitat section to preserve air while losing usable workspace. At the end of the mission, players receive a comprehensive Flight Director Decision Log detailing their survival metrics and the real-world engineering science behind each choice.

Benefits & Intended Impact Space-themed STEM content for children often falls into two extremes: overly simplified arcade games that ignore physical constraints, or dense engineering manuals that overwhelm young minds. Project OrbitOps bridges this gap by making systems engineering trade-offs tangible, visual, and fun. By framing failure and resource scarcity as safe, replayable puzzles, the app builds critical thinking, systems-level problem-solving, and authentic aerospace literacy—inspiring the next generation of students to explore STEM and space exploration careers.

Tools, Languages & Software Used

  • Build Tool & Frontend Stack: Vite, HTML5, CSS3, JavaScript (ES6+), responsive UI/UX dashboard design, and custom SVG/2D habitat graphics.
  • Data Used :
    1)NASA Open APIs — DONKI (Space Weather Database Of Notifications, Knowledge, Information) for real-time solar storm and CME telemetry.
    2)NASA Planetary Data System (PDS) for lunar and Martian surface cartography (Ares Planitia and lunar south pole coordinates).
    3)NASA Mars Science Laboratory (REMS) environmental telemetry for Martian Sol cycles and atmospheric conditions.
    4)NASA Artemis Program mission parameters for lunar surface habitat, power, and life-support trade-offs.
  • Hosting & Version Control: GitHub / GitHub Pages for zero-install, cross-platform browser accessibility, also used Vercel.

Creativity & Key Design Factors Considered

  • Zero Barrier to Entry: Built with Vite as a lightweight, fast-loading web application that runs instantly in any modern browser without downloads, installations, or account sign-ups.
  • Cognitive Load Balancing for Ages 7–12: Instead of overwhelming young players with dozens of complex variables, we focused on core interdependent meters (Power, Oxygen, Water, Crew Health) paired with bite-sized, jargon-free "Science Takeaways" after every decision.
  • Real-World Scientific Grounding: Every game mechanic reflects actual lunar mission protocols, teaching concepts like In-Situ Resource Utilization (ISRU), cumulative astronaut radiation limits, autonomous rover maintenance, and modular habitat isolation.
